segments.text: ​​​ ​Shiori~n!​ ​​
​​​ ​Carpet paws,​ ​​
​​​ ​magic quests,​ ​​
​​​ ​and swimming...​ ​​
​​​ ​In history!​ ​​
​​​ ​During my stay in the Great Wolf Lodge,​ ​​

​​​ ​I'll start off with some fun​ ​​
​​ ​at the hotel and museums​ ​​
​​​ ​before history takes a turn for the spooky.​ ​​

​​​ ​So sit back and relax​ ​​
​​ ​while I begin my vacational yap.​ ​​
​​​ ​Yaaap, yapyapyapyap yaaap.​ ​​

​​​ ​So my parents always wanted to​ ​​
​​ ​visit the Great Wolf Lodge,​ ​​
​​​ ​but it was never in the budget until now.​ ​​

​​​ ​It's a family resort packed with​ ​​
​​ ​a lot of activities to distract your kids.​ ​​
​​​ ​...If you have some.​ ​​
​​​ ​Or you're a giant kid yourself.​ ​​
​​​ ​Bowling alleys, arcades, and even MagiQuest,​ ​​

​​​ ​a game where you wave a customized​ ​​
​​ ​wand at random objects​ ​​
​​​ ​and solve riddles with it.​ ​​

​​​ ​There's also a Build-A-Bear workshop​ ​​
​​ ​next to their merch store,​ ​​
​​​ ​and, of course, the buffet.​ ​​

​​​ ​And if you're an adult, you can just​ ​​
​​ ​laze around in the indoor swimming pool​ ​​
​​​ ​or try out the VR room's minigames.​ ​​
​​​ ​They give you a discount or a voucher​ ​​
​​​ ​just for staying with them for the day,​ ​​

​​​ ​but I forgot about that,​ ​​
​​ ​so I didn't get to try the VR one.​ ​​
​​​ ​Room tour!​ ​​
​​​ ​Okay, no one look.​ ​​

​​​ ​To get inside, they give you a​ ​​
​​ ​plastic bracelet with a chip inside.​ ​​
​​​ ​Just hold it up to the door, and it'll unlock.​ ​​

​​​ ​Once you put the bracelet on,​ ​​
​​ ​it's really hard to remove,​ ​​

​​​ ​so don't put it on too tight,​ ​​
​​ ​or you might regret it just like I did.​ ​​

​​​ ​Once inside, the bathroom is​ ​​
​​ ​immediately to your left or right,​ ​​

​​​ ​followed by a small refreshment​ ​​
​​ ​area stocked with coffee and tea.​ ​​
​​​ ​The sink is actually outside the bathroom,​ ​​

​​​ ​which makes sense because​ ​​
​​ ​the bathroom is pretty small.​ ​​

​​​ ​Not that I have surviving​ ​​
​​ ​footage of it to show you.​ ​​

​​​ ​As for the hotel lobby,​ ​​
​​ ​it has a cool cabin-style setup​ ​​
​​​ ​with the check-in desk underneath.​ ​​
​​​ ​There's also a Dunkin' Donuts right next to it,​ ​​

​​​ ​and a massive fireplace that​ ​​
​​ ​gives the whole place a cozy vibe.​ ​​
​​​ ​Depending on the schedule,​ ​​

​​​ ​they have storytime events and​ ​​
​​ ​small shows for kids there.​ ​​
​​​ ​The lodge also had a mining sluice.​ ​​

​​​ ​Kind of like a hands-on gacha,​ ​​
​​ ​but for sediments and gemstones.​ ​​

​​​ ​You buy a pre-packed bag​ ​​
​​ ​called a "mining rough,"​ ​​

​​​ ​pour it into the wooden tray​ ​​
​​ ​with the mesh bottom,​ ​​
​​​ ​then dip the tray into the water.​ ​​

​​​ ​It's meant to mimic how miners​ ​​
​​ ​would pan for gold or gemstones.​ ​​
​​​ ​Hopefully you end up with something you like.​ ​​
​​​ ​I didn't try it myself, but I can see the appeal.​ ​​
​​​ ​It's tactile, a little messy,​ ​​
​​​ ​and there's the hope of getting a pretty gem.​ ​​

​​​ ​For eateries, it had a buffet open​ ​​
​​ ​for breakfast, lunch, and dinner.​ ​​

​​​ ​The seatings were framed with wooden​ ​​
​​ ​beams and lantern-styled lights,​ ​​
​​​ ​giving it a cozy and rustic vibe.​ ​​

​​​ ​As for food, from what I remember​ ​​
​​ ​there was a small salad bar​ ​​
​​​ ​and mostly meat and carbs.​ ​​

​​​ ​There were some vegetarian options too,​ ​​
​​ ​but I didn't look at that.​ ​​

​​​ ​I had roast beef, mashed potatoes,​ ​​
​​ ​mac and cheese, tater tots...​ ​​
​​​ ​That sort of thing.​ ​​

​​​ ​There was a dessert station with​ ​​
​​ ​pudding cups and rice crispies too,​ ​​
​​​ ​but nothing that stood out for me personally.​ ​​
​​​ ​If none of the food satisfies you,​ ​​

​​​ ​you can take a cab and go to​ ​​
​​ ​the historical town nearby.​ ​​

​​​ ​They have restaurants and a lot of shops​ ​​
​​ ​that you can check out instead.​ ​​
​​​ ​Now that we're done with the hotel tour,​ ​​
​​​ ​it's time for the museum tour.​ ​​

​​​ ​This brick building here is the​ ​​
​​ ​Jamestown museum in Virginia,​ ​​

​​​ ​home to what's known as the first​ ​​
​​ ​successful English colony in America.​ ​​
​​​ ​But it wasn't easy getting there.​ ​​
​​​ ​Disease,​ ​​
​​​ ​starvation, and...​ ​​
​​​ ​even cannibalism nearly wiped out the colony.​ ​​

​​​ ​Yet here we are centuries later,​ ​​
​​ ​walking through the same place​ ​​
​​​ ​by paying around 20 bucks to get in! Whoopee!​ ​​
​​​ ​Get ready for some history info dump.​ ​​

​​​ ​Jamestown was the first permanent​ ​​
​​ ​English settlement in America,​ ​​
​​​ ​established by the Virginia Company.​ ​​

​​​ ​They chose this spot because​ ​​
​​ ​it was easy to defend,​ ​​

​​​ ​and it's right next to the James River,​ ​​
​​ ​so they could spot ships coming in.​ ​​

​​​ ​Unfortunately, the terrain was​ ​​
​​ ​plagued by swampy land,​ ​​
​​​ ​mosquito-born disease (buzz buzz),​ ​​
​​​ ​scarce food, and undrinkable water,​ ​​
​​​ ​making survival brutal.​ ​​
​​​ ​Now, if you ever decide to visit Jamestown,​ ​​
​​​ ​the main appeal is being able to walk around​ ​​

​​​ ​and take in the sights at whatever​ ​​
​​ ​pace you want for yourself.​ ​​

​​​ ​So you're going to see things that resemble​ ​​
​​ ​the structures from way back then.​ ​​
​​​ ​Depending on when you visit,​ ​​

​​​ ​you might be lucky enough to meet​ ​​
​​ ​the historians dressed in period clothing,​ ​​

​​​ ​and they'll share with you what they​ ​​
​​ ​know about the village's history.​ ​​
​​​ ​Inside, things were kept pretty simple.​ ​​

​​​ ​You got wooden tables, cookware,​ ​​
​​ ​armor, equipment...​ ​​
​​​ ​And very little privacy.​ ​​

​​​ ​Such a small space that they had to be​ ​​
​​ ​very particular with what they keep.​ ​​
​​​ ​It would be so over for me, guys.​ ​​

​​​ ​I have way too much merch and​ ​​
​​ ​way too many clothes to live there.​ ​​
​​​ ​Some of the houses did have a second floor,​ ​​

​​​ ​but it was barred off,​ ​​
​​ ​so no idea what's up there.​ ​​
​​​ ​Who knows, maybe they have colonial merch.​ ​​

​​​ ​This house, for example,​ ​​
​​ ​I'm pretty sure belonged to the more rich folks.​ ​​
​​​ ​Maybe you've heard of Captain John Smith,​ ​​
​​​ ​because he led the small colony in its early years.​ ​​

​​​ ​During his leadership, there was this rough​ ​​
​​ ​period known as the "Starving Time."​ ​​

​​​ ​Out of the 500 original settlers,​ ​​
​​ ​only 60 were left alive.​ ​​

​​​ ​Basically supply ships either sank​ ​​
​​ ​or they just arrived way too late,​ ​​
​​​ ​so the colony had no food and was starving.​ ​​
​​​ ​Initially, the Powhatan people traded with settlers.​ ​​
​​​ ​But when Jamestown kept growing and growing,​ ​​

​​​ ​the tribe just couldn't keep up​ ​​
​​ ​with their increasing demands.​ ​​
​​​ ​When trade wasn't enough,​ ​​

​​​ ​the settlers resorted to raiding Powhatan​ ​​
​​ ​villages for food and supplies,​ ​​

​​​ ​even burning some of the houses​ ​​
​​ ​and kidnapping Pocahontas—​ ​​
​​​ ​the daughter of Chief Powhatan—​ ​​
​​​ ​to use as leverage during negotiations.​ ​​
​​​ ​To make things worse,​ ​​

​​​ ​the Powhatan people were killing​ ​​
​​ ​anyone who tried to leave the fort,​ ​​
​​​ ​making hunting and farming impossible.​ ​​
​​​ ​Settlers ended up eating horses, dogs, rats...​ ​​
​​​ ​Even the leather from their shoes.​ ​​
​​​ ​And some accounts even mention cannibalism.​ ​​

​​​ ​Meanwhile, the Powhatan people already had​ ​​
​​ ​homes built to handle the environment.​ ​​

​​​ ​Their yehakins were made from​ ​​
​​ ​woven mats and wooden frames,​ ​​

​​​ ​and you can see some of these​ ​​
​​ ​on the venue if you choose to visit.​ ​​
​​​ ​This is a native American cabin.​ ​​
​​​ ​Inside, it's simple.​ ​​
​​​ ​Pelts spread across beds,​ ​​

​​​ ​maybe even hanging on the walls​ ​​
​​ ​or laid on the floors to insulate the home.​ ​​
​​​ ​Above the beds is what looks like a drying rack,​ ​​
​​​ ​used to hang up hides, furs, or clothes.​ ​​

​​​ ​This tight bundle of sticks may be firewood​ ​​
​​ ​storage or used for some other material.​ ​​
​​​ ​The pelts looked so fuzzy and cozy.​ ​​

​​​ ​I wanted to touch it,​ ​​
​​ ​but I also thought it was probably unclean.​ ​​
​​​ ​That didn't stop Plushvella, though.​ ​​

​​​ ​Despite the early mortality​ ​​
​​ ​rates and the hardships,​ ​​
​​​ ​Jamestown is considered a success,​ ​​

​​​ ​especially once John Rolfe​ ​​
​​ ​introduced tobacco to the economy.​ ​​
​​​ ​With that, let's move on to Yorktown.​ ​​
​​​ ​My museum ticket came bundled with Yorktown,​ ​​

​​​ ​and with the two exhibits close to each other,​ ​​
​​ ​I figured why not visit.​ ​​

​​​ ​When I first entered,​ ​​
​​ ​to my side were marching silhouttes of soldiers,​ ​​
​​​ ​preparing for battle against the British.​ ​​

​​​ ​Yorktown is important, because this was​ ​​
​​ ​about America's fight for independence.​ ​​

​​​ ​And the Battle of Great Bridge is a turning​ ​​
​​ ​point in history as America's first victory.​ ​​

​​​ ​The bridge itself was a key route​ ​​
​​ ​that connected two sides of the river,​ ​​

​​​ ​so it was important to access it​ ​​
​​ ​to control the region.​ ​​
​​​ ​Behold! More words.​ ​​
​​​ ​This is Thomas Jefferson.​ ​​

​​​ ​He's on the nickels and drafted the​ ​​
​​ ​Declaration of Independence,​ ​​
​​​ ​which separated America from Britain.​ ​​

​​​ ​Over there, you got Big Ben—​ ​​
​​ ​famous dirty kite flyer.​ ​​

​​​ ​But nah, aside from electricity,​ ​​
​​ ​he secured the French alliance for Americans.​ ​​

​​​ ​For those who don't know, France and Britain​ ​​
​​ ​have a history of hating each other.​ ​​
​​​ ​There are also notes on the Home Front,​ ​​

​​​ ​which is about how communities​ ​​
​​ ​managed and supported the war effort.​ ​​
​​​ ​Spy networks,​ ​​
​​​ ​writing,​ ​​

​​​ ​and neighborhood efforts​ ​​
​​ ​like farming, sewing, and so on.​ ​​

​​​ ​There was this personality quiz on this giant​ ​​
​​ ​display at some point in the museum.​ ​​
​​​ ​And it was pretty cool, honestly.​ ​​

​​​ ​It asks you maybe five questions​ ​​
​​ ​on how you'd handle these certain situations.​ ​​
​​​ ​And then it matches your answers​ ​​

​​​ ​based on other historical figures​ ​​
​​ ​who did do something similar.​ ​​
​​​ ​This is one of my results,​ ​​

​​​ ​and this person for example​ ​​
​​ ​was a writer, playwright,​ ​​
​​​ ​and a strong critic against British rule.​ ​​

​​​ ​Her writing stirred revolutionary​ ​​
​​ ​sentiment in the colony,​ ​​

​​​ ​and she wrote a history​ ​​
​​ ​of the American Revolution,​ ​​

​​​ ​making her one of the first women​ ​​
​​ ​to provide detailed accounts of war.​ ​​
​​​ ​The museum was packed with a lot information.​ ​​
​​​ ​Plaques about generals,​ ​​
​​​ ​stories from soldiers,​ ​​
​​​ ​tons of historical maps,​ ​​
​​​ ​and even a holographic display​ ​​

​​​ ​where actors reenacted what it was like​ ​​
​​ ​to be a soldier back then.​ ​​

​​​ ​There's also a mini theater that plays​ ​​
​​ ​short historical films at set intervals.​ ​​
​​​ ​I didn't go in for Yorktown,​ ​​

​​​ ​so the footage you're seeing​ ​​
​​ ​is actually from Jamestown​ ​​
​​​ ​and focuses on Bacon's Rebellion.​ ​​

​​​ ​If you ever visit, you can check out​ ​​
​​ ​the theater yourself and catch a little show.​ ​​
​​​ ​Yorktown was honestly a really fun museum.​ ​​

​​​ ​I'm pretty sure this handsome statue​ ​​
​​ ​of George Washington would agree.​ ​​

​​​ ​Outside, they had full recreations​ ​​
​​ ​of military encampments,​ ​​

​​​ ​and I was lucky enough to catch​ ​​
​​ ​some re-enactors in action.​ ​​

​​​ ​They even showed me what people​ ​​
​​ ​ate back in the old ye times.​ ​​
​​​ ​And... She laughed at my jokes, guys.​ ​​
​​​ ​She thought I was funny.​ ​​

​​​ ​Basically, soldiers primarily​ ​​
​​ ​ate bean and meat stew.​ ​​
​​​ ​In that left bowl is a hardtack with split peas.​ ​​

​​​ ​The dry biscuit was meant to last for​ ​​
​​ ​a long time without spoiling,​ ​​
​​​ ​and they would soak it into soup to make it edible.​ ​​
​​​ ​If it's too dry, it can actually break your teeth.​ ​​
​​​ ​There was also a medic (or surgeon)​ ​​

​​​ ​who demonstrated the kinds of​ ​​
​​ ​tools they used back then,​ ​​
​​​ ​which was both cool and a little terrifying.​ ​​
​​​ ​On the table you have a few tools.​ ​​

​​​ ​You have the bone saw,​ ​​
​​ ​used for amputations without any anesthesia.​ ​​

​​​ ​The cautery iron would seal​ ​​
​​ ​the wound with burning hot iron.​ ​​

​​​ ​Bullet extractors.​ ​​
​​ ​They'd remove any shrapnel or musket balls,​ ​​
​​​ ​otherwise you might have an infection.​ ​​
​​​ ​The tooth key.​ ​​

​​​ ​If a tooth was decayed or infected,​ ​​
​​ ​they would wrench it out.​ ​​

​​​ ​They might even accidentally​ ​​
​​ ​break the tooth or jaw during this.​ ​​

​​​ ​And you got a toothbrush.​ ​​
​​ ​Made out of twigs.​ ​​

​​​ ​Oh, and in the back there were some​ ​​
​​ ​farmhouses you could explore.​ ​​

​​​ ​And a cute little cat​ ​​
​​ ​that they told you not to pet.​ ​​

​​​ ​Not sure who the cat belongs to,​ ​​
​​ ​but don't touch it and don't touch the chickens.​ ​​
​​​ ​Yorktown felt way more immersive from outside.​ ​​
​​​ ​They even had a small seasonal farm in the back,​ ​​
​​​ ​plus walking, live rotisserie.​ ​​

​​​ ​One of the houses had a baker​ ​​
​​ ​who explained how they salted meat​ ​​
​​​ ​so that it could last for months.​ ​​

​​​ ​And she even had an example,​ ​​
​​ ​but I couldn't capture the footage of it.​ ​​
​​​ ​Too many people.​ ​​

​​​ ​She was also in the middle​ ​​
​​ ​of baking a pie and, wow,​ ​​
​​​ ​there were some realistic flies buzzing around.​ ​​
​​​ ​Buzz buzz.​ ​​

​​​ ​And lastly, one of the houses had​ ​​
​​ ​dried-up tobacco hanging from the ceiling.​ ​​

​​​ ​They were trying to remove the moisture​ ​​
​​ ​from it to prepare for the markets.​ ​​

​​​ ​So if you like history​ ​​
​​ ​or seeing things from the past,​ ​​

​​​ ​maybe go the museum,​ ​​
​​ ​'cause I had a lot of fun there.​ ​​
​​​ ​Overall, really fun trip at the museum.​ ​​
​​​ ​Yorktown being my favorite between the two.​ ​​

​​​ ​Jamestown and Yorktown are also​ ​​
​​ ​pretty close to Williamsburg.​ ​​

​​​ ​And the triad formed the "Historic Triangle,"​ ​​
​​ ​which is pretty neat.​ ​​

​​​ ​If you're not into museums,​ ​​
​​ ​what about a little ghost hunting instead?​ ​​

​​​ ​At night, Williamsburg takes on​ ​​
​​ ​an entirely different tone.​ ​​
​​​ ​Flickering torchlight,​ ​​
​​​ ​boots echoing on old brick,​ ​​
​​​ ​and guides dressed in colonial wear​ ​​

​​​ ​as they lead you through one of the​ ​​
​​ ​most haunted towns in America.​ ​​

​​​ ​For this ghost tour,​ ​​
​​ ​we were split into three groups​ ​​
​​​ ​and led through three different locations.​ ​​

​​​ ​An old courthouse​ ​​
​​ ​and two preserved colonial homes.​ ​​

​​​ ​For the courthouse,​ ​​
​​ ​the guide told us about the trials held there.​ ​​
​​​ ​Executions, public punishments...​ ​​
​​​ ​Typical stuff from the era.​ ​​
​​​ ​But one story stood out.​ ​​

​​​ ​It was about a homeless man​ ​​
​​ ​with an enormous debt.​ ​​

​​​ ​There wasn't a proper "jail"​ ​​
​​ ​in the town at the time,​ ​​
​​​ ​so when the villagers got tired of him,​ ​​
​​​ ​they locked him up in a makeshift prison​ ​​
​​​ ​while they figured out what to do with him.​ ​​

​​​ ​On one night, when the sheriff's daughter​ ​​
​​ ​came by to bring him food,​ ​​
​​​ ​she heard voices from his cell.​ ​​

​​​ ​It sounded like he was​ ​​
​​ ​having a full conversation,​ ​​

​​​ ​but the voice that he spoke to​ ​​
​​ ​was deeper, slower...​ ​​
​​​ ​Unnatural.​ ​​
​​​ ​After opening the little sliding slot to peek in,​ ​​
​​​ ​she found him standing there,​ ​​

​​​ ​staring right at the wall,​ ​​
​​ ​talking to the "devil."​ ​​
​​​ ​The accounts after that are muddied.​ ​​

​​​ ​No one knows exactly​ ​​
​​ ​what happened to him after.​ ​​

​​​ ​Some stories say he went blind,​ ​​
​​ ​some say he died.​ ​​

​​​ ​As for the girl,​ ​​
​​ ​she was never the same again.​ ​​

​​​ ​After that, we visited the​ ​​
​​ ​Peyton Randolph House,​ ​​

​​​ ​which is considered as the most​ ​​
​​ ​haunted home in all of Williamsburg.​ ​​

​​​ ​It was more of a collection of spirits​ ​​
​​ ​instead of just one restless entity.​ ​​
​​​ ​Stories of children who died young,​ ​​
​​​ ​soldiers who never came home,​ ​​

​​​ ​and silhouettes of people​ ​​
​​ ​dressed from a different time.​ ​​
​​​ ​The last house was smaller,​ ​​

​​​ ​and tucked away in the middle​ ​​
​​ ​of town near a church.​ ​​

​​​ ​Like the other house,​ ​​
​​ ​there was no electricity,​ ​​
​​​ ​only oil lamps to light up the way.​ ​​

​​​ ​There was a checkerboard floor​ ​​
​​ ​in the room we sat in,​ ​​

​​​ ​and the guide shared simpler​ ​​
​​ ​stories to end the night with.​ ​​

​​​ ​Nothing dramatic.​ ​​
​​ ​Just a cozy end to tie up the tour.​ ​​
​​​ ​And that wraps it up!​ ​​
​​​ ​The Wolf Lodge, history walks,​ ​​
​​​ ​battlefield tours, and a ghost or two.​ ​​
​​​ ​So, thanks for watching the video.​ ​​

​​​ ​If you ever decide to visit Williamsburg,​ ​​
​​ ​be sure to check behind you.​ ​​

​​​ ​You never know what you​ ​​
​​ ​may end up leaving with.​ ​​
